## The multiverse has its critics {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- "Robustness is better assessed with a **few thoughtful models** than with billions of regressions" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; answering @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources] – only *justified* models targeting the *same estimand* belong in one curve. Today's grid is a **curated 840**, and the fork chart does the job that every critic endorses: it locates where the argument must happen
- "**There is only one correct analysis**" once the question is fully specified [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne] – your declared specification guards against *cherry-picking*, and their deeper point is that declaring in advance does not yet make a choice *justified*, which is what the estimand and DAG work were for
- "What's a multiverse **good for** anyway?" – reflection, persuasion, or inference, and each purpose needs a *differently built* universe [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood]. Today's was built for **reflection**, and how much more to read into it is the open debate
:::

::: {.src}
The book-length how-to: @YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational; the estimand diagnosis behind Part 2: @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
The method you practised is the subject of a live debate, and you can now read that debate for yourself. Katrin Auspurg, whose estimand diagnosis you met in Part 2, answered a 3.6-billion-estimate study with the line at the top of this slide: only thoughtful, justified models belong in a curve. What we did today mostly agrees with her: our grid is a curated eight hundred and forty, not an enumeration, and the fork chart does the one job that every critic endorses, which is to show where the argument has to happen. Lakens and colleagues say that once the question is fixed, only one analysis implements it correctly. Your preregistration guarded against cherry-picking. Their deeper point, that declaring early does not make a choice justified, is why we built the DAG before declaring. And Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask what a multiverse is for: reflection, persuasion, or inference, each needing a differently built set. Ours was built for reflection, and how much more can be read into it is the open question in the debate you have now joined. [advance]
:::

## "There is only one correct analysis" {.smaller}

::: {.small}
The argument from Lakens and colleagues runs in four steps:

- A research question, **fully specified**, implies a quantity to be estimated
- That quantity, together with the design and the assumptions you are willing to make, implies **one analysis** that estimates it
- So a spread of results is not evidence of legitimate diversity. It is evidence that **most of those specifications are wrong** – they estimate something else
- On this reading, showing a wide curve is closer to an admission than to a robustness check
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Take it back to the red cards. Twenty-nine teams modelled one count of red cards as **linear, logistic or Poisson**. Those are claims about how the outcome was generated, and they cannot all be right – so on this argument most of the spread is error.
:::

::: {.src}
@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne
:::

::: notes
And now the strongest objection to everything I have just taught you, and I want to give it its full force. Lakens and colleagues argue that a research question, once fully specified, implies a quantity to be estimated. That quantity, together with your design and the assumptions you are prepared to make, implies one analysis that estimates it. From which it follows that a spread of results is evidence that most of those specifications are wrong, because they estimate something other than what you said you wanted, and not evidence of legitimate analytical diversity at all. And on that reading, publishing a wide specification curve is closer to an admission that you never specified your question than to a robustness check. That is an uncomfortable argument and I think it is largely right.
:::

## Which analysis, and how you would know {#how-would-you-know .smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Grant the argument, and suppose that **one correct analysis exists**. Which one is it?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Getting there needs the estimand *and* the identification assumptions *and* agreement about the measurement – and on this claim, reasonable people disagree about all three.
:::

::: {.fragment}
So the curve complements the one-correct-analysis view: it is a **map of the disagreement that remains**, drawn because we cannot yet settle it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
And it points at what to argue about: on this claim, at the **outcome**, not at the estimator.
:::
::::

::: notes
So let us grant the argument. Suppose one correct analysis does exist. The next question is which one it is, and how you would know. To get there you need the estimand, and the identification assumptions, and agreement about how the construct is measured – and on this claim reasonable people disagree about all three, as you saw for yourselves this afternoon. So I read the curve as a companion to the one-correct-analysis view rather than a rival to it. It is a map of the disagreement that remains, drawn because we cannot yet settle it. Read that way it is useful, because it shows where the disagreement is. On this claim it is at the outcome – what 'EU framing' means – and not at the estimator, which is where the seminar argument would have been.
:::

## What preregistration settles {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does settle**

- That your specification was not chosen *because of* the result
- That your rule for what counts as support was written before you had one
- That a reader can see what you intended, and what you changed
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does not settle**

- Whether the specification was **any good**
- Whether it estimates the quantity that your question implies
- Whether the assumptions behind it hold

A badly reasoned analysis that is declared in advance is still badly reasoned; the declaration only adds a timestamp
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
That is why the estimand and the DAG came **first** today: preregistration protects a choice, and the causal reasoning is what justifies it.
:::

::: notes
So where does preregistration fit? It settles a specific and limited set of things, and the two columns matter equally. On the left: it settles that your specification was not chosen because of the result it gave, that your rule for what counts as support was written before you had a result to bend it around, and that a reader can see both what you intended and what you subsequently changed. Those are real guarantees and no other mechanism provides them. On the right, what it does not settle: whether the specification was any good, whether it estimates the quantity that your question implies, or whether its assumptions hold. A badly reasoned analysis that is declared in advance is still badly reasoned, only now with a timestamp on it. That is why we did the estimand and the graph first this morning. Preregistration protects a choice, and the causal reasoning is what justifies it.
:::

::: notes
This afternoon you reproduced my constrained result, and then you explored – several specifications, tried in whatever order took your interest, in order to find out what they do. That was the right way to learn them, and I want to be clear that there was nothing improper about it. Now comes the other half. You commit to one specification, declared in writing before it runs, with a reason that your causal graph supports. The code for the two activities is identical. The difference is that one of them can be chosen because of the result it gave, and the other one cannot, and almost no published paper says which of the two it is reporting.
